(Office pantry. Yusuf talks with Anirban, a senior colleague.)

Yusuf: Anirban, can I ask how you think about the loan? I have a list, two columns.

Anirban: Show me.

Yusuf: Left side, the tax deduction on interest. Right side, what carrying the debt costs, and the peace of mind of clearing it.

Anirban: Good. How do you weigh them?

Yusuf: I lean towards prepaying, but I'm not sure.

Anirban: I lean the same way, but my numbers are not yours. My salary and taxes differ. Talk to a fee-only adviser as well.

Yusuf: Fee-only means they don't earn commission on products?

Anirban: Yes. They can look at your real figures.

Yusuf: Then I'll book a session and bring the list.

Anirban: Good. The list is the useful part.

qa.q: What two columns did Yusuf's list have?
qa.a: The left side listed the tax deduction on interest, and the right side listed what carrying the debt costs and the peace of mind of clearing it.

qa.q: What is Yusuf feeling about the decision?
qa.a: Yusuf feels unsure and a little anxious, leaning towards prepaying but not certain.

qa.q: What could Yusuf do with the adviser's answer, and why?
qa.a: Yusuf could compare it with the list and the personal numbers before deciding, because general reasoning must be checked against personal figures.

qa.q: How might Anirban see the request for help?
qa.a: Anirban seems glad to share an opinion but careful to say that personal numbers differ, so an adviser should look.

grounding: A graduate lists interest tax deduction against the cost of carrying debt and asks a colleague and an adviser how they weigh it.

passage:
I'm Reena, and in March I got my first bonus: ₹60,000. The question was whether to put it into my education loan early or keep it.
So I made a list in two columns on the office whiteboard after hours.
For prepaying: less interest over the years, loan finished sooner, one less thing on my mind.
For keeping it: the interest on this loan gets a tax deduction, so it costs a bit less than the rate says; and I have almost no emergency savings.
My senior, Tarun, looked at it and said he'd kept his loan running for the deduction, but his situation was different: he already had savings. Then I booked a session with a fee-only adviser, someone paid by the hour who doesn't sell anything. The adviser asked for my actual numbers and went through them with me.
The list didn't decide for me. But I understood what I was choosing.

qa.q: How much was Reena's first bonus?
qa.a: Reena's first bonus was ₹60,000, in March.

qa.q: How did Reena feel after the session with the adviser?
qa.a: Reena felt clearer and more confident, not because the list decided anything but because the choice was finally understood.

qa.q: Why was it wise for Reena to check with the adviser as well as Tarun?
qa.a: Tarun's choice fit his own savings; a fee-only adviser could test the general reasoning against Reena's actual numbers.

qa.q: Why might Tarun have chosen differently from what suits Reena?
qa.a: Tarun already had savings, so keeping the loan for the deduction carried less risk than it might for Reena.

grounding: Shows a graduate weighing a loan-interest tax deduction against the cost of carrying debt, then asking a senior and a fee-only adviser before choosing.

Mentor's note, 2 May. Abhinav, senior engineer, graduate mentoring scheme.
Shalini brought a pros-and-cons list to our monthly chat. She has an education loan and ₹50,000 saved, and wanted to know whether to prepay part of the loan.
Her list was careful. Against prepaying: the loan interest gives her a tax deduction, and she'd lose most of her emergency cushion. For prepaying: less debt and less interest over time, and, she said, the loan 'sits on my chest'.
She asked what I had done. I told her honestly: I prepaid, but I had no family depending on me and a year's savings already, so my case may not be hers. I suggested she take the same list to a fee-only adviser who would look at her actual figures, and she booked one for next week.
She seemed relieved that nobody expected her to decide today. I'll hear how it went next month.

qa.q: How much does Shalini have saved?
What does Shalini mean when she says the loan 'sits on my chest'?
qa.a: She feels the debt as a heavy, anxious weight, which is part of why prepaying appeals to her.

qa.q: Which step in the note best protects Shalini from a hasty choice?
qa.a: Taking the list to a fee-only adviser who checks her actual figures, rather than copying the mentor's choice.

qa.q: How does the question look to Abhinav, the mentor who wrote the note?
qa.a: Abhinav shares an honest example but sees that different circumstances mean it may not fit, so points Shalini to someone who can check her own numbers.

grounding: Shows a graduate listing tax-deduction and debt-cost pros and cons, hearing a senior's view and booking a fee-only adviser to check personal numbers.
